questions.stem: The phase space of \(N\) point particles moving in three dimensions has dimension:

explanation.whyCorrect: Each particle needs 3 position and 3 momentum coordinates, giving \(6N\) dimensions; a microstate is a single point in this space.

whyWrong.D: Counts one position and one momentum per particle (1D).

explanation.howToModify: Ask for the dimension for \(N\) rigid diatomic molecules (\(10N\)).

questions.stem: Liouville's theorem states that, for a Hamiltonian system, the phase-space density \(\rho\):

options.C: is uniform over all of phase space at all times
options.D: is constant along the trajectory of each phase point

explanation.whyCorrect: \(d\rho/dt = \partial\rho/\partial t + \{\rho, H\} = 0\): the ensemble flows like an incompressible fluid, so phase-space volumes are conserved.

whyWrong.A: Fine-grained density is conserved; Liouville's theorem says nothing about entropy increase.
whyWrong.B: Holds for any Hamiltonian evolution, in or out of equilibrium.
whyWrong.C: Uniformity is an equilibrium (microcanonical) assumption, not Liouville's theorem.

explanation.trapUsed: Confusing the theorem with the equal a priori probability postulate.
explanation.howToModify: Ask for the condition on \(\rho\) for a stationary ensemble (\(\{\rho,H\}=0\)).
explanation.howToAvoid: Liouville is about flow along trajectories (total derivative), not about uniformity.

questions.stem: The phase-space trajectory of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator of fixed energy \(E\) is:

whyWrong.D: Particle in a uniform field (e.g. free fall) in the \(x\)–\(p\) plane gives a parabola.

explanation.trapUsed: Matching potentials with the wrong conic.
explanation.howToModify: Ask for the phase trajectory of a particle in a box (rectangle).
explanation.howToAvoid: Write energy conservation in \(x\) and \(p\) and read off the curve.

questions.stem: For a 1D harmonic oscillator, the phase-space area enclosed by the trajectory of energy \(E\) is \(2\pi E/\omega\). The number of quantum states with energy up to \(E\) is therefore approximately:

explanation.whyCorrect: Each quantum state occupies area \(h\): \(N \approx \frac{2\pi E/\omega}{2\pi\hbar} = E/\hbar\omega\), consistent with \(E_n \approx n\hbar\omega\).

whyWrong.C: The area itself, not divided by \(h\).

explanation.howToModify: Ask for the density of states \(dN/dE\) (\(1/\hbar\omega\)).

questions.stem: In quantum statistical mechanics, the volume of phase space associated with one microstate per degree of freedom is:

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair \((q_i,p_i)\) contributes a cell of area \(h\); for \(f\) degrees of freedom the cell volume is \(h^f\) (so \(h^3\) per particle in 3D).

whyWrong.A: \(h^3\) is per particle in 3D, not per degree of freedom.
whyWrong.B: Minimum uncertainty product, not the cell size.

explanation.trapUsed: Per particle vs per degree of freedom.
explanation.howToModify: Ask why classical entropy contains an arbitrary constant without this cell.
explanation.howToAvoid: One (q, p) pair ↔ one factor of \(h\).

questions.stem: A phase-space density \(\rho(q,p)\) represents a stationary (equilibrium) ensemble whenever:

options.D: \(\rho\) depends on \((q,p)\) only through the Hamiltonian \(H(q,p)\)

explanation.whyCorrect: If \(\rho = \rho(H)\) then \(\{\rho,H\} = \rho'(H)\{H,H\} = 0\), so \(\partial\rho/\partial t = 0\). Microcanonical and canonical ensembles are both of this form.

whyWrong.A: Arbitrary functional form; not stationary in general.
whyWrong.B: Spatial uniformity alone does not guarantee stationarity.
whyWrong.C: Normalization is always required and says nothing about time dependence.

explanation.howToModify: Ask which other conserved quantities \(\rho\) may depend on (e.g. total momentum).
